samples.text:
In many cities, there is not enough space and land is very expensive. Some people think city land should be used mostly for parks and green areas, but others believe it is better to use it for houses and businesses. In this essay, I will discuss both views.

Firstly, parks and green spaces are very important for people who live in cities. They give people a place to relax, do exercise and meet friends. For children, parks are safe places to play, because many families live in small flats without garden. Also, trees help to make the air more cleaner and reduce the temperature in summer. If a city has no green space, people may feel stressed and unhealthy.

Secondly, other people think housing and business are more important. The population of cities is growing fastly, and many people cannot find a home they can afford. If the government build more flats, the prices will go down and young people can live near their work. Businesses also need land for offices, shops and factories, which create jobs for local people. Without jobs, the city cannot develop.

In my opinion, I believe that land should be used for both, but housing is a little more important. People need a home before they can enjoy a park. However, the government should make sure that every new area has at least a small park, so residents have somewhere to go.

In conclusion, parks improve health and environment, while housing and business help people to live and work. I think cities need a balance, but homes should be the first priority.
samples.why: Addresses both views with a stated opinion · relevant ideas but limited extension · formulaic linking (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several comparative, word-form and agreement errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
As urban populations grow, the question of how to use limited city land has become increasingly important. Some people believe it should be devoted mainly to parks and green spaces, while others think housing and commercial development should take priority. In my view, both are essential, but green space should not be sacrificed simply to meet short-term demand for buildings.

Those who favour housing and businesses make a practical argument. In many large cities, property prices have risen so sharply that ordinary workers, such as nurses and teachers, can no longer afford to live near their jobs. Building more homes on available land would help to ease this shortage. In addition, businesses need space for offices and shops, which generate employment and tax revenue. From this perspective, leaving valuable land undeveloped could seem like a luxury that crowded cities can't afford.

On the other hand, supporters of green space argue that parks are not a luxury but a necessity. They provide opportunities for exercise and relaxation, which contributes to both physical and mental health. Trees and plants also improve air quality, reduce flooding by absorbing rainwater, and help to lower temperatures during heatwaves. Once a park is built on, it is almost never restored, so losing green space is effectively permanent.

I believe the solution lies in smarter planning rather than choosing one use over the other. Cities can increase housing by building upwards and redeveloping disused industrial sites, rather than using existing parks. At the same time, new developments should be required to include green areas, so that residents benefit from nature on their doorstep.

In conclusion, while the need for housing and businesses is urgent, I believe cities should protect and expand their green spaces, since they are vital for the long-term wellbeing of residents.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended with relevant examples · logical paragraphing and varied linking · some less common vocabulary (disused industrial sites) · frequent error-free sentences with two minor slips.

samples.text:
Land in cities is a scarce and valuable resource, and how it is allocated shapes the lives of millions of residents. Some argue that it should be used predominantly for parks and other green spaces, whereas others believe that housing and commercial premises should take precedence. In my view, although the demand for homes is pressing, green space must be treated as essential infrastructure rather than as a dispensable amenity.

The case for prioritising housing and business is compelling in many cities. Chronic shortages of affordable accommodation force workers to endure long commutes or to leave urban areas altogether, which harms both their quality of life and the local economy. Commercial development, meanwhile, generates employment, attracts investment and provides the tax revenue that funds public services. Seen from this angle, reserving large areas for parks might appear to be an indulgence that a growing city can ill afford.

However, this reasoning underestimates the tangible value of green space. Parks offer residents, particularly those living in flats without gardens, a place to exercise, socialise and escape the pressures of urban life, with well-documented benefits for physical and mental health. They also perform important environmental functions: vegetation absorbs rainwater, mitigating the risk of flooding, and helps to counteract the heat that builds up in densely built areas. Crucially, once green space is developed, it is rarely, if ever, recovered.

Rather than framing the issue as a stark choice, I believe cities should pursue housing growth in ways that preserve and even enhance green areas. Building at higher densities, redeveloping former industrial land and converting underused offices into homes can all increase supply without encroaching on parks. New developments, in turn, can be required to incorporate gardens, tree-lined streets and shared open spaces.

In conclusion, while the need for homes and businesses is undeniable, green space is too important to be treated as expendable. Careful planning allows cities to meet both needs, but existing parks should be protected rather than sacrificed.
samples.why: Both views fully developed and critically weighed · clear, nuanced position with practical proposals · skilful cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (dispensable amenity, encroaching) · wide range of accurate structures.
